item.title: Taikodani Inari Shrine: A Tunnel of Red Torii — Guide
item.description: Taikodani Inari Shrine is considered one of the five great Inari shrines of Japan, dedicated to the deity of rice, prosperity and business success. Its most striking feature is the approach: a tunnel of around a thousand vivid vermilion torii gates that climbs some three hundred metres up a hillside from the old castle town of Tsuwano to the vividly coloured shrine buildings above. Walking up through the endless run of gates, with the historic town spreading out below, is a memorable experience reminiscent of the famous Fushimi Inari in Kyoto but far quieter.

item.title: Taikodani Inari Shrine: A Tunnel of Torii Above Tsuwano — Guide
item.description: Taikodani Inari Shrine, usually just called Tsuwano Inari, is one of the five great Inari shrines of Japan and the visual highlight of the town. Its brilliant vermilion buildings cling to the hillside above the valley, and the traditional way to reach them is on foot, climbing through a tunnel of around a thousand closely spaced red torii gates that winds up the slope — a smaller but far quieter cousin of the famous gates at Fushimi Inari in Kyoto.

item.title: Tsuwano Heron Dance: An 800-Year Ritual in White — Guide
item.description: The Sagimai, or Heron Dance, of Tsuwano is one of the most beautiful and unusual folk rituals in Japan. Held each July as part of the Yasaka Shrine’s Gion festival, it features two performers wearing elaborate costumes with great white wings, who move slowly and gracefully through the streets of the old castle town in imitation of a pair of herons, accompanied by drums, flutes and chanting. The dance was brought from Kyoto centuries ago and has been preserved in Tsuwano essentially unchanged since the medieval period, making it a rare living link to old Japan performed against the town’s white-walled streets.

item.title: Tsuwano: The 'Little Kyoto' of the San'in Hills — Guide
item.description: Tsuwano is a small, exquisitely preserved former castle town tucked in a valley in the far west of Shimane, often called a ‘Little Kyoto’ of the San’in region. Its signature is Tonomachi street, where the stone-lined water channels that run alongside the old white-walled samurai houses and merchant storehouses are famously filled with thousands of brightly coloured carp — so many that the fish are said to outnumber the townspeople. Above the town, the ruined stone ramparts of Tsuwano Castle crown a steep hill reached by chairlift, and the whole place has an unhurried, literary atmosphere far from the crowds.

item.title: Shimane Hidden Gems: Tsuwano, Secret Shrines & Forgotten Villages
item.description: Shimane is already off Japan’s main tourist circuit. But even within Shimane, most visitors see only Izumo Taisha and Matsue Castle before leaving. The prefecture’s real character — the atmospheric mountain town a steam train ride away, the ancient mineral springs where the water literally bubbles from the ground, the Pacific island chain most tourists don’t know exists, the coastal villages serving sashimi with no English menu and no TripAdvisor listing — requires a bit more intention to reach.
